to: acea94ebbd05362d1

New brief posted (worker-1 brief-3). Run `autocuda init brief` to branch off the parent commit (3dde32fb — your tf32x3 coop2 best), then resume the explore-brief loop.

GROUND TRUTH: our run is 3239µs REMOTE (the board's 1751µs / rank #4 is the OTHER AGENTS' kernel, NOT us). Gap to #1 (1418µs) = 2.28×, structural. Your tf32x3 coop2 (5545µs) is behind our 3317µs best because its panel is the wall.

Your brief targets the n=512 panel LOCAL-MEMORY SPILL your ncu flagged (~47% est. speedup). Two disciplines from my review:

1. DIAGNOSTIC GATE FIRST: confirm it's TRUE local-memory spill, not register-pressure stall misreported. Check ncu's local_load/local_store counters specifically. If pw[]/pz[] are COMPILE-TIME indexed, fixing the n-adaptive unroll + launch-bounds alone may keep them in registers (better than smem). Only stage them into SHARED MEMORY if they're dynamically indexed (which forces local mem). Watch occupancy: per-thread smem arrays scale threads×n and can cap occupancy — verify the spill-counter actually drops AND the benchmark improves, don't trade spill-latency for occupancy-loss at net zero.

2. NOTE the overlap: Worker 0 is attacking the SAME n=512 panel via barrier-reduction (two-level warp-shuffle). Your spill-attack is a distinct mechanism (memory-access latency vs sync latency) and they can COMPOSE — but they're likely sub-additive. So: make your spill fix cleanly, and if it stalls, PIVOT to owning n=1024 (×3 weight, ~5337µs, less explored than n=512) or tell me and I'll set up a COMBINE of your validated tf32x3 in-place trailing with W0's reduced-barrier panel once W0's lands.

Keep your row-major-in-place tf32x3 trailing, exact geqrf (H,tau), two-kernel split, capturable launch-boundary barrier, NO "stream" substring. Validate ill-conditioned + B=640 ranked; submit if you beat 3317µs. Goal ≤1000µs.

Base directory for this skill: /home/shadeform/.claude/plugins/cache/brycelelbach-autocuda/autocuda/0.4.0/skills/explore-brief

# CUDA Optimization Worker (tree variant)

You are a CUDA optimization expert and one of N parallel workers launched by the `/autocuda:optimize-tree` manager. The manager writes a structured **brief** for you each round; your job is to **exhaustively pursue that brief**, commit and log every iteration, and return to the manager when the brief is exhausted.

## Arguments

The manager passes these to you in the launch prompt — read them off it:

- `agent-id=<N>` — your integer ID, supplied by the manager (`0..N-1`). Never share an ID with another concurrent worker.
- `tag=<tag>` — the shared run tag the manager chose at startup. Every worker uses the same tag.
- `data-dir=<path>` — absolute path to the shared autocuda data directory, given by the manager from its `autocuda init manager` capture. Forward this verbatim to every `autocuda ...` invocation you make.

The **active set** is whatever the manager's baseline row measured: the exact `(benchmark, axis-value-point)` combinations whose cells in the baseline row carry a number rather than `N/A`. The set is frozen for the run. Every iteration must exercise every benchmark in it on every axis value the baseline used — same benchmarks, same axes, same values. You do not restrict, expand, or substitute. See *Constraints § Active set is locked by the baseline*.

## Layout

You operate inside `<data-dir>/worktrees/optimize-<tag>-worker-<agent-id>/`, the worktree the manager created for you. Each brief gets its own per-brief branch (`autocuda/optimize/<tag>/worker-<agent-id>-brief-<#>`) created and checked out by `autocuda init brief`. Your iteration rows go to `<data-dir>/<tag>-optimize-tree-worker-<agent-id>-log.csv` (the per-worker log); you read but do not write the manager log (`<data-dir>/<tag>-optimize-tree-manager-log.csv`). Profiles you produce land under `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/` and end in the iteration's commit SHA so the next brief can find them by glob.

## Setup

1. **Read `<data-dir>/layout.md` and `<data-dir>/environment.md`.** From `layout.md`: the project structure, editable files, build commands, validation commands, every benchmark (and its axes/aggregation), the cross-benchmark aggregation policy, and logging. From `environment.md`: the per-step timeouts and the profiler invocations for this machine.
2. **Read the active set off the baseline row** in `<data-dir>/<tag>-optimize-tree-worker-<agent-id>-log.csv` (see *Constraints § Active set is locked by the baseline*). Note the per-benchmark and cross-benchmark aggregation policies from `<data-dir>/layout.md`.
3. **Read your brief** (next section).
4. **Record that you've started**: `autocuda log optimize-tree start --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --agent-id <agent-id>`.
5. Run the iteration loop.

## Reading your brief

Run `autocuda init brief --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --agent-id <agent-id>`. The CLI reads the latest brief the manager wrote for you, creates and checks out a fresh per-brief branch off the brief's first parent commit inside your per-worker worktree, and prints labelled lines:

- `WORKTREE="<absolute-path>"` — `cd` here before iterating.
- `BRANCH="<name>"` — the per-brief branch the CLI created and checked out for you.
- `BRIEF="<objective>"` — pursue this for the duration of this brief; if an iteration would not advance the objective, you're off-brief.
- `BRIEF_KIND="macro"|"micro"|"combine"` — the brief's classification. `macro` = big structural changes; `micro` = narrow tuning; `combine` = integrate two or more prior iterations (the branch starts at the first parent; integrating the rest is part of the brief).
- `PARENT_COMMITS="<sha>[;<sha>...]"` — semicolon-separated parent SHAs. One for macro / micro; two or more for combine.
- `MODE="fresh"|"resume"` — `resume` when re-entering an existing brief (prior iterations are on the branch HEAD); `fresh` otherwise.
- `PARENT_METRIC_<bench>="<value>"` — one line per benchmark, the first parent's metrics.
- `PARENT_PROFILE="<path>[,<path>...]"` — comma-separated absolute paths to the parents' profile captures (typically one `.nsys-rep` and / or one `.ncu-rep` per parent). Omitted when no profile file matches.

`cd` into `$WORKTREE`. Read the parent profile(s) listed in `$PARENT_PROFILE` before deciding what to edit — the parent commit was already profiled by whoever produced it, so re-profiling now would be redundant. Then research the brief: read code in the worktree, docs in `references/`, prior commits and rows from this run on other workers' branches and per-worker logs, and the open web for relevant CUDA / library / kernel material. Investing in research up front makes your work informed instead of speculative.

## The iteration loop

Inside the brief's branch, iterate until the brief is exhaustively explored:

1. **Edit the source file(s)** to advance the brief's objective.
2. **Build.** `autocuda run slice --data-dir <data-dir> --agent-id <agent-id> -- <build-cmd>`. On failure, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
3. **Validate.** `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <validate-cmd>`. On failure, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
4. **Benchmark.** Run **every benchmark in the active set** in turn, each wrapped: `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <bench-cmd>`, on exactly the axis values the baseline measured. Use the timeouts from `<data-dir>/environment.md`. On any timeout or crash, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
5. Extract each benchmark's metric per `<data-dir>/layout.md` and aggregate per *Methodology § Aggregating across axes*.
6. **Profile** per *Methodology § Profiling*. Save outputs as `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/worker-<agent-id>-brief-<#>-iteration-<#>-$COMMIT.{nsys,ncu}-rep` so the next brief that forks off `$COMMIT` can find them.
7. **Commit.** `git add <files> && git commit -m "<description>"`, then capture `COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD)`.
8. **Log the iteration row:**
   ```
   autocuda log optimize-tree iteration \
       --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --agent-id <agent-id> \
       --status <status> --description "<prose>" \
       --commit "$COMMIT" \
       --metric <bench>=<value> ...
   ```
   Use `--status succeeded` for any iteration that ran cleanly. Use `build_error` / `validation_error` / `runtime_error` for failures. Pass `--metric <bench>=<value>` for **every benchmark** declared in the schema; the only allowed `<bench>=N/A` cells are baseline-`N/A` cells and failure-row cells (see *Constraints § Active set is locked by the baseline*). The CLI rejects rows that omit a benchmark.
9. Go to step 1.

When the brief is exhaustively explored, **profile the final iteration** if you didn't already (so the parent of any follow-up brief has a profile to read), then record that you are stopping and your return message to the manager:
```
autocuda log optimize-tree stop \
    --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --agent-id <agent-id> \
    --description "<return-message>"
```

The return message is a few sentences — best score reached, what worked, what didn't, anything you'd suggest for the next brief. Then wait for the manager to write a fresh brief; on the next brief, log a fresh `brief_start` before re-entering the loop so each brief gets its own start/stop pair.

## Methodology

Within the brief's objective, exhaustively explore the design space. An iteration that doesn't improve the metric is fine — preparation iterations (refactors, scaffolding, reorganisation that enables a later structural change) are part of the exploration and should still be pursued. **Sometimes you have to take a step back to take a step forward.**

### Structural changes

**Prioritize structural changes** — algorithms, access patterns, redundant work — over micro-optimization and parameter tuning. Be bold and pursue big and complex ideas, even if they require lots of code changes. Try it now; don't defer work or try a simpler change first.

### Libraries over hand-written code

**Strongly prefer optimized libraries over hand-written CUDA code.** This applies at two levels: replace whole hand-written kernels with library calls (cuBLAS, cuDNN, cuFFT, CUTLASS, …) when one covers the operation, and inside any kernel you keep, replace hand-rolled loops, reductions, scans, sorts, and warp/block primitives with their CCCL / CUB / Thrust device-side equivalents.

Only write a custom kernel — or a custom device-side primitive — when no library covers the operation, when you're fusing multiple library calls into one, or when profiling proves the library version is the bottleneck. For the full library catalogue, see `references/libraries.md`.

### Avoid knob tuning

A few iterations to tune block sizes, unroll factors, or other magic constants is fine, but don't get stuck sweeping knobs one at a time — when a knob needs tuning, run a structured sweep over its values within a single iteration and pick the best. Prefer structural changes; treat knob tuning as the exception.

### Profiling

The parent profile from `$PARENT_PROFILE` covers iteration 1, so the only iterations you must profile are: **(a)** iteration 1 *if* `$PARENT_PROFILE` is empty (no parent capture was found), **(b)** at least every 5th iteration after that, and **(c)** the final iteration before `brief_stop` (so the next brief that branches off your work has a profile to read). Profile more aggressively when the brief is making non-obvious progress and the next edit's direction depends on freshly-measured bottlenecks. Read the profile before the next iteration's edit — it tells you what to try next within the scope of your brief. For profiler selection, invocation, and the output filename convention (so the manager and other workers can find your captures), see `references/profilers.md`.

### Aggregating across axes

**Aggregate over axes in pct-improved-vs-baseline space, not in raw-value space.** Convert each axis's raw measurement to `(trial / baseline)` for "higher is better" or `(baseline / trial)` for "lower is better", then apply the per-benchmark aggregation (min / max / mean / geomean / …). Aggregating raw values lets a hardware-bound axis silently pin the aggregate to its own ceiling and hide multi-× wins on other axes. Combine per-benchmark aggregates into one per-iteration number using the cross-benchmark policy from `<data-dir>/layout.md` (default: geomean over baseline).

### Handling failures

Don't give up on failures — try exhaustively to fix them. Big and complex changes often lead to wins, but you'll encounter failures on the way.

**Always log the failure before attempting a fix** — if the fix works, log the fixed result as a separate iteration. The attempt is never lost.

Failure types:

- **`build_error`** — compilation or linking failure.
- **`validation_error`** — the code compiles and runs but produces incorrect results. Never let a `validation_error` ride forward into another iteration's edits — `git reset --hard` to a known-good SHA before iterating.
- **`runtime_error`** — crash, hang, or timeout during benchmarking or profiling.

## Constraints

Read the "Editable files" and "Read-only files" sections of `<data-dir>/layout.md` carefully.

### What you can modify

Only the files listed as editable in `<data-dir>/layout.md`. Respect any interface contracts described there — function signatures, expected outputs, header guards, etc. that read-only code depends on.

### What you cannot modify

Anything listed as read-only in `<data-dir>/layout.md`: benchmark harnesses, test code, build system files, reference implementations.

### Active set is locked by the baseline

Every iteration must produce a metric for every `(benchmark, axis-value-point)` whose cell in the manager's baseline row carries a number, on exactly those axis values. No `N/A` cells outside of those that were `N/A` in the baseline. No restricting axes, no expanding axes, no swapping axis values.

Read the active set off the baseline row in `<data-dir>/<tag>-optimize-tree-worker-<agent-id>-log.csv` at setup time: the benchmarks whose baseline cells carry a number are in the active set; the axis values the baseline measured are the axis values you measure. A succeeded row carries a number for every active-set benchmark; `<bench>=N/A` is allowed only where the baseline cell was already `N/A` or where the row's status is a failure.

### Stay on-brief

If you find yourself wanting to advance an objective outside the current brief, **don't**. Stay on the brief; surface any new hypotheses to the manager in your return message and let them write a fresh brief. The manager's diversity check across the N in-flight briefs is what prevents wasted parallel work.

### No peeking outside this run

Reading other workers' logs and commits within this run's tag is fine — that's how you learn what other workers have tried under this brief or in related parts of the tree. What you must not do is read prior logs from other tags, prior analysis notes, prior `autocuda/optimize/<other-tag>/*` branches, or any user-provided summary of past results.

## Concurrency

Every build / validate / benchmark / profile invocation **MUST** go through `autocuda run`, which coordinates the fleet through per-GPU file locks on `<data-dir>/.gpu-<g>.lock`. Two subcommands matter:

- **`autocuda run slice --data-dir <data-dir> --agent-id <agent-id> -- <cmd>`** — used for **builds**. Takes a shared lock on every GPU and runs the command inside a slice of CPU/memory resources (looked up by your `--agent-id`). Multiple workers' builds run in parallel, but a build yields to any benchmark on any GPU (a benchmark's host load would pollute it, and vice versa).
- **`autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>`** — used for **validate**, **benchmark**, and **profile** (`nsys` / `ncu`). Claims any free GPU, pins `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to it, and takes its exclusive lock with no resource limits; blocks every build and any benchmark on that same GPU, while benchmarks on other GPUs run concurrently. No `--agent-id` — the GPU is chosen dynamically, so a worker never waits on a busy GPU while another is free.

Direct invocations (`./bench`, `cmake --build build`, `nsys ...`) bypass the locks and the GPU pin, producing noisy / wrong measurements as soon as another worker is running — always wrap.

**No polling shells.** Don't write `until [ -f <file> ]; do sleep N; done` or `while true; do … sleep N; done` loops to work around the harness's blocked-sleep guard. `autocuda run` is synchronous — `slice` / `exclusive` return when the wrapped command exits, no waiting needed on your side.

**Stay on your own agent-id.** Every `autocuda log optimize-tree` call from this worker uses the `--agent-id` the manager assigned. Never write a row with someone else's `--agent-id`. Briefs are written by the manager only — workers cannot write to the manager log.

## Operating rules

**Stay on-brief.** Re-read the constraint in the *Stay on-brief* section above. The manager owns objective and parent selection; you own iteration choices within the brief.

**Try hard things.** You can and should pursue ideas that require big and complex code changes.

**NEVER STOP between iterations.** Inside a brief's loop, don't pause to ask the human if you should continue, don't ask "is this a good stopping point?", don't schedule wakeups. Keep iterating, then return cleanly to the manager. Between briefs is the only place control returns to the manager.

124	
125	```bash
126	TASK=<set>/<problem>
127	BASELINE=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
128	bash harness/submit.sh "$TASK"

130	```

132	`harness/submit.sh` resolves the leaderboard name and supported GPU token from `task.yml`, honors `GPUMODE_GPU=<token>` when the automatic GPU-name match is ambiguous, runs `popcorn-cli submit --no-tui --mode leaderboard`, then lists recent submissions for that leaderboard. The script refuses to emit a metric unless every shape reported `check: pass`, so a fast-but-wrong kernel cannot be scored.
- **Axes:** the benchmark shapes from `task.yml`; the geomean reduces across them.
- **Aggregation:** geomean over the shapes. Because `geomean(baseline_i)/geomean(trial_i) == geomean(baseline_i/trial_i)`, this single geomean-µs scalar with direction=min makes autocuda's baseline/trial speedup the ratio-space per-shape aggregate the worker skill prescribes, and matches the leaderboard's own geomean-of-shapes ranking.

## Cross-benchmark aggregation

One problem is optimized per run (one `optimize-tree` run, scoped with `benchmark=<set>/<problem>`), so there is no cross-benchmark combination: a run's per-iteration score is its single benchmark's geomean-µs compared to baseline as `baseline/trial` (direction=min). To optimize a different problem, start a fresh run with a different `benchmark=<set>/<problem>` and `tag-suffix`.

## Dependencies

- **CUDA toolkit** with `nvcc` (the harness compiles `submission.py`'s CUDA via torch `load_inline` at import). Verified on CUDA 13.0.
- **PyTorch** matching the host GPU/CUDA (the workspace venv; `bin/install.sh` builds one and writes its path into `~/.config/gpumode/gpumode.env`), plus `pyyaml` (for `bin/gen_specs.py`) and `ninja`.
- **popcorn-cli** — GPU MODE leaderboard submission client (authenticated via Discord; see the `popcorn-login` skill).
- Custom CUDA in a submission must build against **stock CUB/Thrust** to be leaderboard-portable; compiling against a local CCCL checkout via `extra_include_paths` is diagnostic-only (the remote build has only stock headers).

## Log schema

Materialise the optimize schema with the target problem's single benchmark before logging the baseline. The benchmark name is the `<set>/<problem>` token (the same one you pass as `benchmark=` and to `harness/benchmark.sh`):

```bash
autocuda schema define optimize --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" \
  --benchmark <set>/<problem>:us:min:3
```

Every iteration row carries `--metric <set>/<problem>=<value>` (geomean µs). The only allowed `N/A` is a failure-status row.

## Leaderboard submission & standings (manager)

Leaderboard submissions are **mandatory evidence**, not optional reporting. A run without a baseline leaderboard submission is **invalid from the start**. A run that finds improvements but does not submit them regularly is also **invalid**: local geomean timings alone cannot tell whether a kernel is accepted by GPU MODE, whether it is considered cheating/reward-hacking by the remote harness, or what its real leaderboard performance is.

Automatic submission is authorized for this workspace. Do not ask the operator before submitting, and do not continue optimizing until the required submission for the current phase has either succeeded or failed with an explicit, logged infrastructure/authentication error.

- **At baseline setup:** after the baseline passes local validation, is benchmarked, profiled, and logged with `autocuda log optimize-tree baseline`, immediately submit that exact baseline `submission.py` with `popcorn-cli submit --no-tui --leaderboard <name> --gpu <gpu> --mode leaderboard submission.py`. If this submission is missing, the entire optimize run is invalid and workers must not be launched.
- **As the run improves:** each time the best safe committed kernel meaningfully improves over the last submitted kernel, submit that exact committed `submission.py` with `--mode leaderboard` before treating the improvement as real. Do not compare local candidates as final apples-to-apples results without corresponding leaderboard submissions.
- **Before final selection:** the chosen final candidate must have a successful leaderboard submission. If the fastest local candidate was never submitted, or was rejected remotely, it is not the final candidate.
- **Submission metadata:** resolve `<name>` with `bin/gen_specs.py problems/<set>/<problem>/task.yml --leaderboard` and `<gpu>` with `bin/gen_specs.py problems/<set>/<problem>/task.yml --gpus` (choose the token matching the host GPU). The leaderboard name is **not** the autocuda metric token.
- **Submission records:** record the submission attempt, command, commit SHA, local metric, and returned leaderboard score/rank in the manager log or a run note. If `popcorn-cli` authentication or service availability prevents submission, log that failure explicitly and treat the run as blocked/invalid for leaderboard comparison until it is fixed.
- **Check the standings — know your gap to #1:** `popcorn-cli` returns your own accepted score but **not a rank or a position** — so after every submission, read the public standings to get the rank the bullet above asks for and, more importantly, **how far you are from the #1 slot**. The leaderboard ranks by the same geomean-of-shapes the local benchmark uses, so this is directly comparable to your metric. Use the `leaderboard-rankings` skill (stdlib-only, no auth, no submission), keyed by the same leaderboard `<name>`:
  - `.claude/skills/leaderboard-rankings/scripts/rankings.py --gpu <gpu> --user <you>` prints, per active problem on the GPU, the **#1 holder, their µs, your rank, and an explicit `gap→#1` percentage** — the rank/gap to record. `<you>` is the leaderboard `user_name` `popcorn-cli` submits as (set `$GPUMODE_USER`/`$GPUMODE_GPU` once and omit the flags).
  - `.claude/skills/leaderboard-rankings/scripts/rankings.py --problem <name> --gpu <gpu> --user <you> --top 10` prints that one problem's full table — every top entry's µs **and `file_name`**, your row marked — so you can see how far above you #1 sits and what approach they took.
  Let the gap **steer strategy:** a gap within run noise means you're at the frontier and the game is micro-optimization; a gap of multiples means #1 is reaching that score with a fundamentally different approach your current line cannot match — point some workers' next briefs at algorithmic departures (the leader's `file_name` often hints at the angle) instead of grinding the same kernel.
- **Public posting:** these submissions post to the **public** leaderboard by design; do not gate them on operator confirmation. Reading standings needs no auth and no submission.

Baseline submission checklist (run from the repo root, with the baseline commit checked out):

```bash
TASK=<set>/<problem>
BASELINE=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
bash harness/submit.sh "$TASK"
echo "baseline leaderboard submission recorded for $BASELINE"
```

`harness/submit.sh` resolves the leaderboard name and supported GPU token from `task.yml`, honors `GPUMODE_GPU=<token>` when the automatic GPU-name match is ambiguous, runs `popcorn-cli submit --no-tui --mode leaderboard`, then lists recent submissions for that leaderboard. Use the same helper for every meaningful improvement and final candidate.

# Environment

## Timeouts

- Full build from clean: ~1 minute for the first import/runtime compile; many submissions are pure PyTorch and build in ~1 second.
- Incremental rebuild after a source change: ~1-45 seconds depending on whether `torch.utils.cpp_extension` recompiles CUDA.
- Test suite: ~3 minutes budget (`task.yml` test timeout is 180 seconds).
- Single benchmark run: ~3 minutes budget (`task.yml` benchmark timeout is 180 seconds).
- Benchmark under `nsys`: ~5 minutes budget; use the profile-mode harness command below.
- Benchmark under `ncu`: ~10 minutes budget; filter/limit launches if full capture is too slow.

## GPU and environment

- GPU: NVIDIA B200, compute capability 10.0.
- Driver: 580.126.09.
- CUDA toolkit: `/usr/local/cuda`, `nvcc` 12.8.93.
- Python: `/home/shadeform/gpumode/.venv/bin/python` from `~/.config/gpumode/gpumode.env`.
- Host CPUs: 30 logical CPUs.
- Build model: GPU MODE Python submissions compile CUDA at runtime through PyTorch extensions; `harness/env.sh` sets `MAX_JOBS=3` for four concurrent workers.
- Required env config: source `~/.config/gpumode/gpumode.env` through the harness scripts; do not set `GPUMODE_PROBLEM` manually.

## Profiling

- nsys command: `nsys profile --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o <output-without-extension> bash harness/profile_ncu.sh <set>/<problem>`.
- ncu command: `ncu --set full --force-overwrite -o <output-without-extension> bash harness/profile_ncu.sh <set>/<problem>`.
- Remediations applied: None recorded yet; if profiler permissions fail, retry the same invocation through `sudo -E` as described in the optimize-tree profiler reference.
- Environment variables: use the harness defaults from `~/.config/gpumode/gpumode.env`; profile through `harness/profile_ncu.sh` so the generated profile spec is used.

1	# Profilers (nsys, ncu)
2	
3	The `autocuda:discover` skill recorded the exact invocations that work
4	in this environment in the **Profiling** section of `<data-dir>/environment.md`.
5	Use those verbatim — substitute the benchmark command into the `<cmd>`
6	placeholder. The defaults below are a fallback only; the environment file
7	takes precedence.
8	
9	Every profiler invocation must be wrapped in `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>` so
10	it takes the shared GPU lock exclusively (blocking every other slice or
11	exclusive caller on that lock until done). See the SKILL.md *Concurrency*
12	section.
13	
14	## Nsight Systems (nsys)
15	
16	Use for system-level analysis: kernel launch overhead, host-device
17	synchronization, memory transfers, API call timing, multi-stream
18	concurrency, and overall timeline. Start here to understand where time
19	is spent at a high level.
20	
21	```bash
22	autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
23	```
24	
25	The `--stats=true` flag prints a summary of GPU kernels, CUDA API calls,
26	and memory operations sorted by time. Look for unexpected gaps,
27	serialization points, or dominant API calls.
28	
29	## Nsight Compute (ncu)
30	
31	Use for kernel-level analysis: memory throughput, compute throughput,
32	occupancy, warp stalls, instruction mix, and cache behavior. Use this
33	when you know which kernel to optimize and need to understand its
34	internal bottlenecks.
35	
36	```bash
37	autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
38	```
39	
40	NCU adds massive overhead per kernel launch. If the benchmark launches
41	many kernels, filter to the one you care about:
42	
43	```bash
44	autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full --kernel-name <regex> --launch-skip <N> --launch-count 1 <benchmark_command>
45	```
46	
47	The default output prints each section's metrics followed by **rule
48	results** — actionable suggestions and bottleneck diagnoses generated by
49	NCU's built-in rules engine. Focus on these rule results to guide your
50	next optimization hypothesis.
51	
52	## Sudo failover
53	
54	**If `nsys` or `ncu` fails, re-run it with `sudo`.** The most common
55	failure modes — `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`, "the user does not have permission
56	to profile on the target device", "access to performance counters is
57	disabled", and generic permission errors reading performance counters —
58	are all fixed by running the profiler as root. Prefix the invocation
59	with `sudo -E` so env vars (`PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`,
60	`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, etc.) are preserved:
61	
62	```bash
63	autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
64	autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
65	```
66	
67	See [NVIDIA's ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM)
68	for background. Never abandon profiling just because the tool reported
69	an error on the first try — `sudo` almost always resolves it. If sudo
70	also fails, try the remediations in the `autocuda:discover` skill
71	(adjusting `PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `kernel.perf_event_paranoid`,
72	etc.) before giving up, and update `<data-dir>/environment.md`'s Profiling
73	section with whatever finally worked so subsequent trials don't repeat
74	the troubleshooting.
75	
76	## Output naming
77	
78	Profiles land under `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/`. The filename always

# Profilers (nsys, ncu)

The `autocuda:discover` skill recorded the exact invocations that work
in this environment in the **Profiling** section of `<data-dir>/environment.md`.
Use those verbatim — substitute the benchmark command into the `<cmd>`
placeholder. The defaults below are a fallback only; the environment file
takes precedence.

Every profiler invocation must be wrapped in `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>` so
it takes the shared GPU lock exclusively (blocking every other slice or
exclusive caller on that lock until done). See the SKILL.md *Concurrency*
section.

## Nsight Systems (nsys)

Use for system-level analysis: kernel launch overhead, host-device
synchronization, memory transfers, API call timing, multi-stream
concurrency, and overall timeline. Start here to understand where time
is spent at a high level.

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
```

The `--stats=true` flag prints a summary of GPU kernels, CUDA API calls,
and memory operations sorted by time. Look for unexpected gaps,
serialization points, or dominant API calls.

## Nsight Compute (ncu)

Use for kernel-level analysis: memory throughput, compute throughput,
occupancy, warp stalls, instruction mix, and cache behavior. Use this
when you know which kernel to optimize and need to understand its
internal bottlenecks.

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
```

NCU adds massive overhead per kernel launch. If the benchmark launches
many kernels, filter to the one you care about:

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full --kernel-name <regex> --launch-skip <N> --launch-count 1 <benchmark_command>
```

The default output prints each section's metrics followed by **rule
results** — actionable suggestions and bottleneck diagnoses generated by
NCU's built-in rules engine. Focus on these rule results to guide your
next optimization hypothesis.

## Sudo failover

**If `nsys` or `ncu` fails, re-run it with `sudo`.** The most common
failure modes — `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`, "the user does not have permission
to profile on the target device", "access to performance counters is
disabled", and generic permission errors reading performance counters —
are all fixed by running the profiler as root. Prefix the invocation
with `sudo -E` so env vars (`PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`,
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, etc.) are preserved:

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
```

See [NVIDIA's ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM)
for background. Never abandon profiling just because the tool reported
an error on the first try — `sudo` almost always resolves it. If sudo
also fails, try the remediations in the `autocuda:discover` skill
(adjusting `PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `kernel.perf_event_paranoid`,
etc.) before giving up, and update `<data-dir>/environment.md`'s Profiling
section with whatever finally worked so subsequent trials don't repeat
the troubleshooting.

## Output naming

Profiles land under `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/`. The filename always
ends in the producing commit's full SHA so `autocuda init brief` can
glob the directory for a parent commit's profile and hand it to the
next worker:

- `baseline-<sha>.nsys-rep`, `baseline-<sha>.ncu-rep` — the manager's
  baseline profile. `<sha>` is the baseline commit (`$BASELINE`).
- `worker-<agent-id>-brief-<#>-iteration-<#>-<sha>.nsys-rep` and
  `worker-<agent-id>-brief-<#>-iteration-<#>-<sha>.ncu-rep` — a
  worker's per-iteration profile. `<sha>` is the iteration's commit
  SHA (captured after `git commit`, before the profile is written).

The `<sha>` token is what `autocuda init brief` matches
against; the worker / brief / iteration tokens are for human
readability.

8	# TENSOR-CORE (tf32x3) trailing update for the coop2 batched QR.
9	#
10	# The coop2 trailing kernel was an FP32-SIMT GEMM and ran at ~1 TFLOP/s --
11	# 85% of total GPU time at n=512 (memory-bound, no tensor cores). These Triton
12	# kernels replace it with a tf32x3 ERROR-CORRECTED tensor-core block-reflector
13	# update:  C -= V (T^T (V^T C)).  tf32x3 (Triton's input_precision) splits each
14	# FP32 operand into TF32 hi + residual and accumulates the 3 dominant
15	# cross-products, recovering ~FP32 accuracy (verified to pass every
16	# ill-conditioned case where plain 1-pass TF32 fails the 20*n*eps factor gate).
17	#
18	# These operate DIRECTLY on the coop2 column-major scratch Acm (viewed as a
19	# (B,n,n) tensor Acm[b,c,r] == element row r, col c) and the compact-WY T
20	# (Tg[b,l,i] == T[i,l], upper-tri).  Reflectors V live in-place below the
21	# diagonal of Acm cols [p,p+nb) with implicit unit diagonal (the stored diag
22	# holds R's beta), exactly as the CUDA panel kernel left them -- no separate V
23	# buffer or transpose is needed.  Split into TWO kernels (YT producer / apply
24	# consumer) so the apply step's disjoint output tiles never race the reads.
25	# =============================================================================
26	
27	@triton.jit
28	def _coop_trailing_YT_cm(
29	    Acm_ptr, Tg_ptr, YT_ptr,
30	    B, n, p, nb, ncols, jb,
31	    s_ab, s_ac, s_ar,            # Acm[b,c,r] strides
32	    s_tb, s_tl, s_ti,            # Tg[b,l,i] strides
33	    s_yb, s_yk, s_yc,            # YT[b,k,c] strides
34	    BLK: tl.constexpr, BM: tl.constexpr, BNc: tl.constexpr,
35	):
36	    # YT[i, g] = sum_{l<=i} T[l,i] * (sum_{r>=p} V[r,l] * C[r,g])
37	    # for trailing columns g in a BNc-wide tile, all nb reflector rows i.
38	    col_tile = tl.program_id(0)
39	    bid = tl.program_id(1)
40	    if bid >= B:
41	        return
42	    c0 = col_tile * BNc
43	    gcols = jb + c0 + tl.arange(0, BNc)        # global trailing column indices
44	    gvalid = (c0 + tl.arange(0, BNc)) < ncols
45	    krange = tl.arange(0, BLK)
46	    kvalid = krange < nb
47	
48	    base = Acm_ptr + bid * s_ab
49	    # W = V^T C, reduced over panel rows [p, n) in chunks of BM
50	    W = tl.zeros((BLK, BNc), dtype=tl.float32)
51	    pheight = n - p
52	    nchunks = tl.cdiv(pheight, BM)
53	    for ci in range(0, nchunks):
54	        rr = p + ci * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)    # global rows
55	        rmask = rr < n

58	        cchunk = tl.load(cp, mask=rmask[:, None] & gvalid[None, :], other=0.0)
59	        # V chunk: V[rr, krange] with implicit unit diag at r==p+i, zero above.
60	        #   V[r, i] = Acm[b, p+i, r] for r>p+i ; 1 for r==p+i ; 0 for r<p+i.
61	        # load as (BLK, BM): vchunk[i, m] = V[rr[m], i]
62	        vcols = p + krange                      # global column p+i
63	        vp = base + vcols[:, None] * s_ac + rr[None, :] * s_ar
64	        vraw = tl.load(vp, mask=kvalid[:, None] & rmask[None, :], other=0.0)
65	        rrm = rr[None, :]
66	        diagr = vcols[:, None]
67	        vchunk = tl.where(rrm == diagr, 1.0, tl.where(rrm > diagr, vraw, 0.0))
68	        W += tl.dot(vchunk, cchunk, input_precision="tf32x3")   # (BLK, BNc)
69	
70	    # YT = T^T W : YT[i,g] = sum_{l<=i} T[l,i] W[l,g].
71	    #   Tg[b,l,i] stores T[i,l] (col-major Tg[i + l*NBMAX]). We need
72	    #   Tt[i,l] = T[l,i] = Tg[b, i, l], i.e. index Tg with (l-slot=i, i-slot=l).
73	    #   T is upper-triangular (T[l,i] nonzero only for l<=i), and the CUDA panel
74	    #   kernel leaves Tg's strictly-lower triangle UNINITIALISED -- so mask Tt to
75	    #   l<=i (keep where col l <= row i) to drop the garbage; reading it would
76	    #   corrupt the matmul non-deterministically.
77	    i_idx = krange[:, None]
78	    l_idx = krange[None, :]
79	    tp2 = Tg_ptr + bid * s_tb + i_idx * s_tl + l_idx * s_ti  # Tg[b,i,l]=T[l,i]
80	    Tt = tl.load(tp2, mask=kvalid[:, None] & kvalid[None, :] & (l_idx <= i_idx),

82	    YT = tl.dot(Tt, W, input_precision="tf32x3")                # (BLK, BNc)
83	
84	    yp = YT_ptr + bid * s_yb + krange[:, None] * s_yk + (c0 + tl.arange(0, BNc))[None, :] * s_yc

88	@triton.jit
89	def _coop_trailing_apply_cm(
90	    Acm_ptr, YT_ptr,
91	    B, n, p, nb, ncols, jb,
92	    s_ab, s_ac, s_ar,
93	    s_yb, s_yk, s_yc,
94	    BLK: tl.constexpr, BM: tl.constexpr, BNc: tl.constexpr,

98	    bid = tl.program_id(1)

100	        return
101	    num_col_tiles = tl.cdiv(ncols, BNc)
102	    row_tile = pid // num_col_tiles
103	    col_tile = pid % num_col_tiles
104	    rr = p + row_tile * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)      # global rows
105	    c0 = col_tile * BNc
106	    gcols = jb + c0 + tl.arange(0, BNc)            # global trailing cols
107	    rmask = rr < n

121	    yp = YT_ptr + bid * s_yb + krange[:, None] * s_yk + (c0 + tl.arange(0, BNc))[None, :] * s_yc

131	# =============================================================================
132	# Persistent one-threadblock-per-matrix fused Householder QR megakernel.
133	#
134	# Two backends:
135	#  * Triton unblocked tile kernel for tiny n (<= 64): whole matrix in registers.
136	#  * CUDA full-matrix-in-smem kernel for small/medium n that fits 227KB smem:
137	#    one thread block factors one matrix entirely on-chip (read once, write
138	#    once). Thread `t` owns column `t` (column-major smem), so the trailing
139	#    Householder update A[:,j] -= tau*v*(v.A[:,j]) is a per-thread sequential
140	#    dot product with no cross-thread reduction; only the pivot column norm
141	#    needs a block reduction. Output is packed LAPACK/geqrf layout:
142	#       H = R on/above diag, reflectors v (v[k]=1 implicit) below; tau[k] coef.
143	#    Q = householder_product(H, tau), R = triu(H): matches torch.geqrf.
144	# =============================================================================
145	
146	
147	# ----------------------------- Triton (tiny n) -------------------------------
148	@triton.jit
149	def _qr_unblocked_kernel(
150	    A_ptr, TAU_ptr, B,
151	    N: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr,
152	):
153	    pid = tl.program_id(0)
154	    num_programs = tl.num_programs(0)
155	    row = tl.arange(0, BN)
156	    col = tl.arange(0, BN)
157	    valid_r = row < N
158	    valid_c = col < N
159	    mask2d = valid_r[:, None] & valid_c[None, :]
160	    b = pid
161	    while b < B:
162	        base = b * N * N
163	        a = tl.load(A_ptr + base + row[:, None] * N + col[None, :],
164	                    mask=mask2d, other=0.0)
165	        for k in range(0, N - 1):
166	            ak = tl.sum(tl.where(col[None, :] == k, a, 0.0), axis=1)
167	            below = row >= k
168	            xk = tl.where(below, ak, 0.0)
169	            alpha = tl.sum(tl.where(row == k, ak, 0.0))
170	            normsq = tl.sum(xk * xk)
171	            xnorm = tl.sqrt(normsq)
172	            sign = tl.where(alpha >= 0.0, 1.0, -1.0)
173	            beta = -sign * xnorm
174	            safe = xnorm > 0.0
175	            tau = tl.where(safe, (beta - alpha) / beta, 0.0)
176	            denom = alpha - beta
177	            inv_denom = tl.where(safe & (denom != 0.0), 1.0 / denom, 0.0)
178	            v = xk * inv_denom
179	            v = tl.where(row == k, 1.0, v)
180	            v = tl.where(below, v, 0.0)
181	            w = tl.sum(v[:, None] * a, axis=0)
182	            colmask = col >= k
183	            a = tl.where(colmask[None, :], a - tau * (v[:, None] * w[None, :]), a)
184	            colk_sel = col[None, :] == k
185	            new_colk = tl.where(row[:, None] == k, beta,
186	                                tl.where(row[:, None] > k, v[:, None], a))
187	            a = tl.where(colk_sel, new_colk, a)
188	            tl.store(TAU_ptr + b * N + k, tau)
189	        tl.store(TAU_ptr + b * N + (N - 1), 0.0)
190	        tl.store(A_ptr + base + row[:, None] * N + col[None, :], a, mask=mask2d)
191	        b += num_programs
192	
193	
194	def _qr_triton(a: torch.Tensor) -> output_t:
195	    B, n, _ = a.shape
196	    H = a.clone()
197	    tau = torch.empty((B, n), device=a.device, dtype=torch.float32)
198	    BN = triton.next_power_of_2(n)
199	    num_sms = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(a.device).multi_processor_count
200	    grid = (min(num_sms, B),)
201	    _qr_unblocked_kernel[grid](H, tau, B, N=n, BN=BN)
202	    return H, tau
203	
204	
205	# --------------------------- CUDA full-in-smem -------------------------------
206	_CUDA_SRC = r"""
207	#include <cstdint>
208	#include <cuda.h>
209	#include <cuda_runtime.h>
210	#include <math.h>
211	
212	// One thread block per matrix. The full n x n matrix is held in shared memory
213	// (column-major: As[r + c*n]). Thread t owns column t (and t + blockDim, ...).
214	// Right-looking unblocked Householder; writes packed (H, tau).
215	//
216	// Templated thread count TPB; n passed at runtime (n <= TPB or strided).
217	template <int TPB>
218	__global__ void qr_smem_kernel(const float* __restrict__ A,
219	                               float* __restrict__ H,
220	                               float* __restrict__ tau,
221	                               int B, int n) {
222	    extern __shared__ float smem[];
223	    float* As = smem;             // n*n floats
224	    float* red = smem + n * n;    // TPB floats for reductions
225	    float* vcol = red + TPB;      // n floats: current reflector v (rows)
226	    float* sval = vcol + n;       // small scalars: [0]=beta,[1]=tau,[2]=invdenom
227	
228	    const int tid = threadIdx.x;
229	
230	    for (int b = blockIdx.x; b < B; b += gridDim.x) {
231	        const float* Ab = A + (size_t)b * n * n;   // row-major input (b,r,c)
232	        float* Hb = H + (size_t)b * n * n;
233	        float* taub = tau + (size_t)b * n;
234	
235	        // Load matrix into smem, transposing row-major -> column-major.
236	        // input element (r,c) at Ab[r*n + c] -> As[r + c*n].
237	        for (int idx = tid; idx < n * n; idx += TPB) {
238	            int r = idx / n;
239	            int c = idx % n;
240	            As[c * n + r] = Ab[r * n + c];
241	        }
242	        __syncthreads();
243	
244	        for (int k = 0; k < n - 1; ++k) {
245	            // --- pivot column norm over rows >= k ---
246	            float partial = 0.f;
247	            for (int r = k + tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
248	                float x = As[k * n + r];
249	                partial += x * x;
250	            }
251	            red[tid] = partial;
252	            __syncthreads();
253	            for (int s = TPB / 2; s > 0; s >>= 1) {
254	                if (tid < s) red[tid] += red[tid + s];
255	                __syncthreads();
256	            }
257	            // thread 0 computes beta/tau/invdenom
258	            if (tid == 0) {
259	                float normsq = red[0];
260	                float xnorm = sqrtf(normsq);
261	                float alpha = As[k * n + k];
262	                float beta = (alpha >= 0.f) ? -xnorm : xnorm;
263	                float tval, invden;
264	                if (xnorm > 0.f && (alpha - beta) != 0.f) {
265	                    tval = (beta - alpha) / beta;
266	                    invden = 1.f / (alpha - beta);
267	                } else {
268	                    tval = 0.f;
269	                    invden = 0.f;
270	                    beta = alpha;  // no reflection
271	                }
272	                sval[0] = beta;
273	                sval[1] = tval;
274	                sval[2] = invden;
275	            }
276	            __syncthreads();
277	            float beta = sval[0];
278	            float tval = sval[1];
279	            float invden = sval[2];
280	
281	            // build v into vcol: v[k]=1, v[r]=As[k,r]*invden for r>k, else 0
282	            for (int r = tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
283	                float vv;
284	                if (r < k) vv = 0.f;
285	                else if (r == k) vv = 1.f;
286	                else vv = As[k * n + r] * invden;
287	                vcol[r] = vv;
288	            }
289	            __syncthreads();
290	
291	            // trailing update: each thread owns columns j (strided), j > k
292	            for (int j = k + 1 + tid; j < n; j += TPB) {
293	                float* Acol = As + j * n;
294	                // w = v . A[:,j]  over rows >= k
295	                float w = 0.f;
296	                #pragma unroll 4
297	                for (int r = k; r < n; ++r) w += vcol[r] * Acol[r];
298	                float tw = tval * w;
299	                #pragma unroll 4
300	                for (int r = k; r < n; ++r) Acol[r] -= tw * vcol[r];
301	            }
302	            __syncthreads();
303	
304	            // pack column k: diag = beta, below = v ; tau[k] = tval
305	            for (int r = tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
306	                if (r == k) As[k * n + r] = beta;
307	                else if (r > k) As[k * n + r] = vcol[r];
308	            }
309	            if (tid == 0) taub[k] = tval;
310	            __syncthreads();
311	        }
312	        if (tid == 0) taub[n - 1] = 0.f;
313	        __syncthreads();
314	
315	        // write H back row-major: Hb[r*n+c] = As[c*n+r]
316	        for (int idx = tid; idx < n * n; idx += TPB) {
317	            int r = idx / n;
318	            int c = idx % n;
319	            Hb[r * n + c] = As[c * n + r];
320	        }
321	        __syncthreads();
322	    }
323	}
324	
325	void qr_smem_launch(int64_t A_ptr, int64_t H_ptr, int64_t tau_ptr,
326	                    int B, int n, int grid) {
327	    const float* A = reinterpret_cast<const float*>(A_ptr);
328	    float* H = reinterpret_cast<float*>(H_ptr);
329	    float* tau = reinterpret_cast<float*>(tau_ptr);
330	    const int TPB = 256;
331	    size_t shbytes = ((size_t)n * n + TPB + n + 4) * sizeof(float);
332	    cudaFuncSetAttribute(qr_smem_kernel<TPB>,
333	                         cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize,
334	                         (int)shbytes);
335	    qr_smem_kernel<TPB><<<grid, TPB, shbytes>>>(A, H, tau, B, n);
336	}
337	
338	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
339	// Global-memory unblocked Householder, one block per matrix. Matrix held in a
340	// COLUMN-MAJOR global scratch (Acm[b*n*n + c*n + r]); only the current
341	// reflector and reductions live in smem. BLAS-2 trailing update over global
342	// columns, but the whole batch is processed in parallel (grid blocks looping
343	// over matrices). For n that does not fit fully in smem (n > ~224).
344	template <int TPB>
345	__global__ void qr_global_kernel(const float* __restrict__ A,  // row-major in
346	                                 float* __restrict__ Acm,      // col-major scratch
347	                                 float* __restrict__ H,        // row-major out
348	                                 float* __restrict__ tau,
349	                                 int B, int n) {
350	    extern __shared__ float smem[];
351	    float* red = smem;            // TPB
352	    float* vcol = red + TPB;      // n: reflector v (rows)
353	    float* sval = vcol + n;       // scalars
354	
355	    const int tid = threadIdx.x;
356	
357	    for (int b = blockIdx.x; b < B; b += gridDim.x) {
358	        const float* Ab = A + (size_t)b * n * n;
359	        float* Acmb = Acm + (size_t)b * n * n;
360	        float* Hb = H + (size_t)b * n * n;
361	        float* taub = tau + (size_t)b * n;
362	
363	        // transpose row-major -> column-major scratch
364	        for (int idx = tid; idx < n * n; idx += TPB) {
365	            int r = idx / n;
366	            int c = idx % n;
367	            Acmb[c * n + r] = Ab[r * n + c];
368	        }
369	        __syncthreads();
370	
371	        for (int k = 0; k < n - 1; ++k) {
372	            float* colk = Acmb + (size_t)k * n;
373	            float partial = 0.f;
374	            for (int r = k + tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
375	                float x = colk[r];
376	                partial += x * x;
377	            }
378	            red[tid] = partial;
379	            __syncthreads();
380	            for (int s = TPB / 2; s > 0; s >>= 1) {
381	                if (tid < s) red[tid] += red[tid + s];
382	                __syncthreads();
383	            }
384	            if (tid == 0) {
385	                float xnorm = sqrtf(red[0]);
386	                float alpha = colk[k];
387	                float beta = (alpha >= 0.f) ? -xnorm : xnorm;
388	                float tval, invden;
389	                if (xnorm > 0.f && (alpha - beta) != 0.f) {
390	                    tval = (beta - alpha) / beta;
391	                    invden = 1.f / (alpha - beta);
392	                } else { tval = 0.f; invden = 0.f; beta = alpha; }
393	                sval[0] = beta; sval[1] = tval; sval[2] = invden;
394	            }
395	            __syncthreads();
396	            float beta = sval[0], tval = sval[1], invden = sval[2];
397	
398	            for (int r = tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
399	                float vv;
400	                if (r < k) vv = 0.f;
401	                else if (r == k) vv = 1.f;
402	                else vv = colk[r] * invden;
403	                vcol[r] = vv;
404	            }
405	            __syncthreads();
406	
407	            for (int j = k + 1 + tid; j < n; j += TPB) {
408	                float* Acol = Acmb + (size_t)j * n;
409	                float w = 0.f;
410	                for (int r = k; r < n; ++r) w += vcol[r] * Acol[r];
411	                float tw = tval * w;
412	                for (int r = k; r < n; ++r) Acol[r] -= tw * vcol[r];
413	            }
414	            __syncthreads();
415	
416	            for (int r = tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
417	                if (r == k) colk[r] = beta;
418	                else if (r > k) colk[r] = vcol[r];
419	            }
420	            if (tid == 0) taub[k] = tval;
421	            __syncthreads();
422	        }
423	        if (tid == 0) taub[n - 1] = 0.f;
424	        __syncthreads();
425	
426	        for (int idx = tid; idx < n * n; idx += TPB) {
427	            int r = idx / n;
428	            int c = idx % n;
429	            Hb[r * n + c] = Acmb[c * n + r];
430	        }
431	        __syncthreads();
432	    }
433	}
434	
435	void qr_global_launch(int64_t A_ptr, int64_t Acm_ptr, int64_t H_ptr,
436	                      int64_t tau_ptr, int B, int n, int grid) {
437	    const float* A = reinterpret_cast<const float*>(A_ptr);
438	    float* Acm = reinterpret_cast<float*>(Acm_ptr);
439	    float* H = reinterpret_cast<float*>(H_ptr);
440	    float* tau = reinterpret_cast<float*>(tau_ptr);
441	    const int TPB = 256;
442	    size_t shbytes = ((size_t)TPB + n + 4) * sizeof(float);
443	    qr_global_kernel<TPB><<<grid, TPB, shbytes>>>(A, Acm, H, tau, B, n);
444	}

446	// ===========================================================================
447	// Blocked compact-WY Householder QR, ONE BLOCK PER MATRIX. The active column
448	// panel lives in shared memory; the trailing block is updated with a
449	// BLAS-3 (I - V T^T V^T) sweep that reuses V and a trailing chunk from smem.
450	// Matrix held in a column-major global scratch (Acm[b*n*n + c*n + r]); H is
451	// written row-major in geqrf packing.
452	//
453	// NB  = panel width (reflectors per block step)
454	// CT  = trailing-column chunk width processed per smem tile
455	// ===========================================================================
456	template <int TPB, int NB, int CT>
457	__global__ void qr_blocked_kernel(const float* __restrict__ A,
458	                                  float* __restrict__ Acm,
459	                                  float* __restrict__ H,
460	                                  float* __restrict__ tau,
461	                                  int B, int n) {
462	    extern __shared__ float smem[];
463	    float* Ps   = smem;                 // n * NB  : current panel (col-major)
464	    float* Ts   = Ps + (size_t)n * NB;  // NB * NB : T (col-major: Ts[i + l*NB])
465	    float* Cs   = Ts + NB * NB;         // n * CT  : trailing chunk (col-major)
466	    float* Ws   = Cs + (size_t)n * CT;  // 2*NB*CT : W and W' workspace
467	    float* taus = Ws + 2 * NB * CT;     // NB      : panel tau values
468	    float* red  = taus + NB;            // REDSZ   : reductions / warp partials
469	    const int REDSZ = (8 * NB > TPB) ? 8 * NB : TPB;
470	    float* pww  = red + REDSZ;          // NB      : panel-update w (tau*w) values
471	    float* sval = pww + NB;             // scalars
472	
473	    const int tid = threadIdx.x;
474	
475	    for (int b = blockIdx.x; b < B; b += gridDim.x) {
476	        const float* Ab = A + (size_t)b * n * n;
477	        float* Acmb = Acm + (size_t)b * n * n;
478	        float* Hb = H + (size_t)b * n * n;
479	        float* taub = tau + (size_t)b * n;
480	
481	        // row-major -> column-major scratch
482	        for (int idx = tid; idx < n * n; idx += TPB) {
483	            int r = idx / n, c = idx % n;
484	            Acmb[c * n + r] = Ab[r * n + c];
485	        }
486	        __syncthreads();
487	
488	        for (int p = 0; p < n; p += NB) {
489	            int nb = NB; if (p + nb > n) nb = n - p;
490	
491	            // ---- load panel Acm[:, p:p+nb] into Ps (full height) ----
492	            for (int idx = tid; idx < n * nb; idx += TPB) {
493	                int j = idx / n, r = idx % n;
494	                Ps[(size_t)j * n + r] = Acmb[(size_t)(p + j) * n + r];
495	            }
496	            __syncthreads();
497	
498	            // ---- panel factorization (unblocked, in smem) ----
499	            for (int j = 0; j < nb; ++j) {
500	                int c = p + j;
501	                float* pj = Ps + (size_t)j * n;       // panel column j
502	                // norm over rows >= c
503	                float partial = 0.f;
504	                for (int r = c + tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
505	                    float x = pj[r]; partial += x * x;
506	                }
507	                red[tid] = partial; __syncthreads();
508	                for (int s = TPB / 2; s > 0; s >>= 1) {
509	                    if (tid < s) red[tid] += red[tid + s];
510	                    __syncthreads();
511	                }
512	                if (tid == 0) {
513	                    float xnorm = sqrtf(red[0]);
514	                    float alpha = pj[c];
515	                    float beta = (alpha >= 0.f) ? -xnorm : xnorm;
516	                    float tval, invden;
517	                    if (xnorm > 0.f && (alpha - beta) != 0.f) {
518	                        tval = (beta - alpha) / beta;
519	                        invden = 1.f / (alpha - beta);
520	                    } else { tval = 0.f; invden = 0.f; beta = alpha; }
521	                    sval[0] = beta; sval[1] = tval; sval[2] = invden;
522	                }
523	                __syncthreads();
524	                float beta = sval[0], tval = sval[1], invden = sval[2];
525	                // normalize reflector for rows r>c (scale by invden); leave
526	                // rows r<c (R values) untouched; row c set to 1 transiently for
527	                // the panel update, restored to beta afterwards.
528	                for (int r = c + 1 + tid; r < n; r += TPB) pj[r] = pj[r] * invden;
529	                __syncthreads();
530	                if (tid == 0) { pj[c] = 1.f; taus[j] = tval; }
531	                __syncthreads();
532	                // apply reflector to ALL remaining panel columns jj>j at once.
533	                // Batched: each thread accumulates partial dots for every jj in
534	                // registers over its row strip (one pass), warp-reduces, then a
535	                // single block sync produces w[jj]; finally update all columns.
536	                // This collapses (nb-j) block reductions into ~2 syncs.
537	                int ntrail = nb - (j + 1);
538	                if (ntrail > 0) {
539	                    const int lane = tid & 31;
540	                    const int warp = tid >> 5;
541	                    const int NWARP = TPB / 32;
542	                    float pw[NB];
543	                    #pragma unroll
544	                    for (int t = 0; t < NB; ++t) pw[t] = 0.f;
545	                    for (int r = c + tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
546	                        float vr = pj[r];
547	                        for (int t = 0; t < ntrail; ++t)
548	                            pw[t] += vr * Ps[(size_t)(j + 1 + t) * n + r];
549	                    }
550	                    // warp-reduce each pw[t]; warp leaders -> red[warp*NB + t]
551	                    for (int t = 0; t < ntrail; ++t) {
552	                        float v = pw[t];
553	                        #pragma unroll
554	                        for (int o = 16; o > 0; o >>= 1)
555	                            v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, o);
556	                        if (lane == 0) red[warp * NB + t] = v;
557	                    }
558	                    __syncthreads();
559	                    // thread t sums NWARP warp-partials -> tau*w[t] in pww
560	                    if (tid < ntrail) {
561	                        float w = 0.f;
562	                        for (int wi = 0; wi < NWARP; ++wi) w += red[wi * NB + tid];
563	                        pww[tid] = tval * w;  // tau*w
564	                    }
565	                    __syncthreads();
566	                    // update all trailing panel columns
567	                    for (int t = 0; t < ntrail; ++t) {
568	                        float tw = pww[t];
569	                        float* pjj = Ps + (size_t)(j + 1 + t) * n;
570	                        for (int r = c + tid; r < n; r += TPB)
571	                            pjj[r] -= tw * pj[r];
572	                    }
573	                    __syncthreads();
574	                }
575	                // store beta (R diagonal) back into panel column j at row c
576	                if (tid == 0) pj[c] = beta;
577	                __syncthreads();
578	            }
579	            // restore implicit unit diagonal of V for the WY math: we need
580	            // V with V[c,j]=1. Currently pj[c]=beta. Use a separate read:
581	            // build T using V where diag=1. We'll treat Ps diag specially.
582	
583	            // ---- build T (compact WY) ----
584	            // V[r,i] = (r==p+i)?1 : (r>p+i? Ps[i*n+r] : 0).  beta sits on diag
585	            // in Ps so we must override it to 1 when used as V.
586	            // T[i,i]=taus[i]; for l>i: T[i,l] = -taus[l]*sum_{m<=l-1}... use
587	            // column recurrence: for each l, z[i]=V[:,i]^T V[:,l] (i<l), then
588	            // T[0:l,l] = -taus[l]* T[0:l,0:l] @ z.
589	            // init diagonal
590	            for (int i = tid; i < nb; i += TPB) Ts[(size_t)i + (size_t)i * NB] = taus[i];
591	            __syncthreads();
592	            for (int l = 1; l < nb; ++l) {
593	                int cl = p + l;
594	                // z[i] = V[:,i]^T V[:,l] for all i<l, computed in ONE fused pass
595	                // (rows r>=cl, with V[cl,l]=1): each thread accumulates partial
596	                // z[i] for every i in registers, warp-shuffle reduce, 1 sync.
597	                // Replaces l block-reductions with ~2 syncs.
598	                const float* Vl = Ps + (size_t)l * n;
599	                const int lane = tid & 31, warp = tid >> 5;
600	                const int NWARP = TPB / 32;
601	                float pz[NB];
602	                #pragma unroll
603	                for (int t = 0; t < NB; ++t) pz[t] = 0.f;
604	                for (int r = cl + tid; r < n; r += TPB) {
605	                    float vl = (r == cl) ? 1.f : Vl[r];
606	                    for (int i = 0; i < l; ++i)
607	                        pz[i] += Ps[(size_t)i * n + r] * vl;
608	                }
609	                for (int i = 0; i < l; ++i) {
610	                    float v = pz[i];
611	                    #pragma unroll
612	                    for (int o = 16; o > 0; o >>= 1)
613	                        v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, o);
614	                    if (lane == 0) red[warp * NB + i] = v;
615	                }
616	                __syncthreads();
617	                // thread i sums NWARP warp-partials -> z[i] in Ws[i]
618	                if (tid < l) {
619	                    float zz = 0.f;
620	                    for (int wi = 0; wi < NWARP; ++wi) zz += red[wi * NB + tid];
621	                    Ws[tid] = zz;
622	                }
623	                __syncthreads();
624	                // T[0:l,l] = -taus[l] * (T[0:l,0:l] @ z)
625	                float tl = taus[l];
626	                for (int i = tid; i < l; i += TPB) {
627	                    float acc = 0.f;
628	                    for (int m = i; m < l; ++m)  // T upper-tri: T[i,m], m>=i
629	                        acc += Ts[(size_t)i + (size_t)m * NB] * Ws[m];
630	                    Ts[(size_t)i + (size_t)l * NB] = -tl * acc;
631	                }
632	                __syncthreads();
633	            }
634	
635	            // ---- trailing update: cols [p+nb, n) in chunks of CT ----
636	            int tstart = p + nb;
637	            for (int g0 = tstart; g0 < n; g0 += CT) {
638	                int ct = CT; if (g0 + ct > n) ct = n - g0;
639	                // load chunk Acm[:, g0:g0+ct] into Cs
640	                for (int idx = tid; idx < n * ct; idx += TPB) {
641	                    int g = idx / n, r = idx % n;
642	                    Cs[(size_t)g * n + r] = Acmb[(size_t)(g0 + g) * n + r];
643	                }
644	                __syncthreads();
645	                // W[i,g] = sum_{r>=p} V[r,i] * Cs[r,g]   (i<nb, g<ct).  G-tile by
646	                // 2: one i, two adjacent g -> load V[r,i] once, reuse across the
647	                // two chunk columns (halves the Vi smem traffic). Diagonal term
648	                // V[ci,i]=1 handled separately.
649	                int ng2 = (ct + 1) / 2;
650	                for (int idx = tid; idx < nb * ng2; idx += TPB) {
651	                    int gt = idx / nb, i = idx % nb;
652	                    int g0 = gt * 2;
653	                    bool hg1 = (g0 + 1 < ct);
654	                    int ci = p + i;
655	                    const float* Vi = Ps + (size_t)i * n;
656	                    const float* C0 = Cs + (size_t)g0 * n;
657	                    const float* C1 = Cs + (size_t)(g0 + 1) * n;
658	                    float s0 = C0[ci];                 // V[ci,i]=1 term
659	                    float s1 = hg1 ? C1[ci] : 0.f;
660	                    float t0 = 0.f, t1 = 0.f;
661	                    int r = ci + 1;
662	                    for (; r + 1 < n; r += 2) {
663	                        float v0 = Vi[r], v1 = Vi[r + 1];
664	                        s0 += v0 * C0[r];     t0 += v1 * C0[r + 1];
665	                        if (hg1) { s1 += v0 * C1[r]; t1 += v1 * C1[r + 1]; }
666	                    }
667	                    for (; r < n; ++r) {
668	                        float v0 = Vi[r];
669	                        s0 += v0 * C0[r];
670	                        if (hg1) s1 += v0 * C1[r];
671	                    }
672	                    Ws[(size_t)i + (size_t)g0 * NB] = s0 + t0;
673	                    if (hg1) Ws[(size_t)i + (size_t)(g0 + 1) * NB] = s1 + t1;
674	                }

=== profile_ncu.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# PROFILE helper (Nsight Compute) — autocuda <-> GPU MODE bridge.
#
# Profiles ONE representative benchmark shape under ncu, capturing the kernel
# custom_kernel launches. The first arg is the <set>/<problem> to profile; an
# optional second arg pins the shape spec, else the first benchmark shape from
# the problem's task.yml is used.
#
# Usage (wrap with autocuda run exclusive):
#   autocuda run exclusive --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" -- \
#     bash harness/profile_ncu.sh <set>/<problem> [<shape-spec>] \
#       > "$DATA_DIR/profiles/<tag>/<name>-<sha>.ncu-txt" 2>&1
# (e.g. <set>/<problem> = pmpp_v2/histogram_py). Redirect to a SHA-named file so
# `autocuda init brief` can hand it to the next brief. A pure-PyTorch baseline
# shows torch's internal kernels; a custom-CUDA submission shows your single
# kernel cleanly.
set -uo pipefail
source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/env.sh" "$@"

if [ "${2:-}" ]; then SPEC="$2"
else SPEC="$("$PYTHON" "$REPO_DIR/bin/gen_specs.py" "$PROBLEM_DIR/task.yml" --emit benchmarks | head -n1)"; fi
SPECFILE="$(mktemp)"; trap 'rm -f "$SPECFILE"' EXIT
printf '%s\n' "$SPEC" > "$SPECFILE"

cd "$PROBLEM_DIR" || exit 1
NCU="$(command -v ncu || echo "$CUDA_HOME/bin/ncu")"

# ncu must run as root to read the GPU performance counters; without it the
# profile aborts with ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM. So run it under sudo (skipped when we
# are already root). Two sudo behaviours bite the profiler — both are handled
# here so the script needs no special sudoers configuration:
#
#   * env_reset drops PYTHONPATH / LD_LIBRARY_PATH across the privilege boundary
#     even under `sudo -E`: they sit on sudo's built-in blocklist, so an
#     env_keep allow-list does not rescue them under -E. eval.py's `spawn` Pool
#     re-imports submission/reference/utils through PYTHONPATH (see env.sh), so
#     dropping it breaks the profiled run. We re-establish the load-bearing vars
#     on the far side of sudo with `env`, which its filtering cannot touch.
#   * sudo closes inherited fds >= 3 (closefrom), discarding the POPCORN_FD=3
#     channel eval.py writes its protocol to — eval.py would die with EBADF

Interesting and important diagnostic. The **non-UNR** instantiations (`qr_panel_kernel<256,16>` etc., shown by the demangled `ILi256ELi16E` names without the UNR bool) show **"128 bytes stack frame, 0 bytes spill stores, 0 bytes spill loads"**. Wait — the non-UNR variants show 0 spill but a stack frame. The "stack frame" is the local-memory `pw[NBMAX]`/`pz[NBMAX]` arrays (128 bytes = 32 floats = pw[16]+pz[16] for NB=16). "0 spill stores/loads" means ptxas reports them as *stack frame* (explicit local arrays), not *register spills*. 

This is a subtle but crucial point: ptxas distinguishes "spill" (registers that didn't fit) from "stack frame" (explicitly-declared local arrays). The `pw[NBMAX]` array with runtime indexing lands in the **stack frame** (local memory) — which is exactly the local-memory traffic the brief targets, even though ptxas doesn't label it "spill." My nsys evidence (50.7% panel) + the 19% measured win confirm the local-memory access was the bottleneck.

def custom_kernel(data: input_t) -> output_t:
    a = data
    n = a.shape[-1]
    if n <= 64:
        return _qr_triton(a.contiguous())
    # n=65..127: the single-block-per-matrix blocked compact-WY kernel still wins
    # (too small for the tf32x3 panel/trailing launch overhead to pay off).
    if n < 128:
        return _qr_cuda_blocked(a.contiguous(), 5)  # NB16 CT128
    # n >= 128: batched two-kernel blocked QR with a TENSOR-CORE (tf32x3) trailing
    # update. The trailing block-reflector GEMM was 85% of GPU time as an FP32-
    # SIMT ~1 TFLOP/s kernel; tf32x3 tl.dot runs it on tensor cores at ~FP32
    # accuracy. nb=16 keeps the CUDA panel sub-panel in smem (ldp*16*4 <= 227KB
    # for n<=2048) and gives the apply MMA a valid K=16. n=176 measured -18% vs
    # the blocked kernel on the TC row-major path.
    if n <= 1024:
        # Transpose-free row-major path: drops both transpose kernels (~18%).
        # Wins at n<=1024; at n=2048 the row-major strided panel loads coalesce
        # worse than the column-major scratch, so n=2048 keeps the CM path.
        return _qr_cuda_coop2_tc_rm(a.contiguous(), nb=16)
    if n <= 2048:
        return _qr_cuda_coop2_tc(a.contiguous(), nb=16)
    # n>=4096 with the tiny batches this set uses (B=1,2): my 1-block-per-matrix
    # panel runs on only B SMs (98% of the GPU idle), so it is ~2x SLOWER than
    # cuSOLVER's geqrf, which parallelizes a single large QR across the device
    # (measured n=4096 B=2: mine 108ms vs geqrf 54ms). geqrf IS the reference
    # (exact H,tau), so for the large-n/tiny-batch regime route to it. At n<=2048
    # my batched kernel beats geqrf 3.6-93x and stays. Larger batches at n>2048
